why_angle: The cited rivals (Volt & Valley, both Tested Watts pages) say outright they run no tests and rank by makers' undated peak or surge figures; this page tables named reviewers' measured overload and motor-start results per pound (DJI Power 1000 V2 cut out just over 3,000 W and started an induction bandsaw, DELTA 3 Plus held 2,600 W for about a minute, OUPES Mega 1 sagged voltage instead of surging) beside the only maker that puts a time on its overload rating.

page.title: Which Power Station Can Start the Biggest Appliances for Its Size
page.h1: Which power station can start the biggest appliances for its size?
page.desc: Rated, surge and measured overload watts per pound for six compact power stations, with the named tester or maker behind each figure and which makers state a surge duration.
page.answer: Short answer. The power station that can start the biggest appliances for its size is the DJI Power 1000 V2: rated 2,600 W continuous, it ran to about 3,000 W before cutting out (95 W per lb) and started an induction-motor bandsaw. The EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus held 2,600 W for about a minute.

page.after:
What the differences mean

Dealectric does not test units. Every figure here is the maker's stated figure or a named reviewer's result, and every per-pound figure is arithmetic on those numbers:

  • DJI Power 1000 V2: 3,000 W ÷ 31.5 lb = 95 W/lb at the measured cut-out; 2,600 W ÷ 31.5 lb = 83 W/lb at its continuous rating.
  • EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus: 2,600 W ÷ 27.6 lb = 94 W/lb, held about a minute. Per pound it ties the DJI; the DJI reaches about 400 W higher before it cuts out.
  • Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2: 2,000 W ÷ 24.9 lb = 80 W/lb.
  • OUPES Mega 1: 2,000 W ÷ 27.8 lb = 72 W/lb.
  • BLUETTI Elite 100 V2: 1,800 W ÷ 25.3 lb = 71 W/lb. By bulk it leads: 32.0 × 21.5 × 25.0 cm = 17.2 L, and 1,800 W ÷ 17.2 L = 105 W/L, against the Anker's 2,000 W ÷ 19.5 L (15.12 × 8.19 × 9.61 in) = 103 W/L.
  • BLUETTI Elite 30 V2: 600 W ÷ 9.5 lb = 63 W/lb.
  • Advertised surge per pound, for comparison: OUPES 4,500 ÷ 27.8 = 162; Elite 100 V2 3,600 ÷ 25.3 = 142; DJI V2 4,400 ÷ 31.5 = 140; DELTA 3 Plus 3,600 ÷ 27.6 = 130; Anker 3,000 ÷ 24.9 = 120 W/lb. None of these peaks comes with a time, and the order flips once held watts are used.
What you want to startFits
Induction-motor shop tools (14-inch bandsaw), a 1,800 W mitre saw, a 12,000 BTU portable ACDJI Power 1000 V2, the only one here with named motor-start results
The same 2,600 W class of load in a lighter unitEcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus, 3.9 lb lighter, held 2,600 W for about a minute {buy:ecoflow-delta-3-plus-1024wh}
Loads that start and run within 1,800 W, where the smallest, lightest box mattersBLUETTI Elite 100 V2, 17.2 L and 25.3 lb {buy:bluetti-elite-100-v2}
A cast-iron table saw, a well pump or a central AC compressorNone of these: The Technology Man's DJI V2 tripped on a table saw, so plan on a larger station
Laptops, phones, fans, lightsBLUETTI Elite 30 V2 (600 W)

Who measured what, and who puts a time on surge

A motor pulls several times its running watts for the moment it takes to spin up. A station starts it only if the inverter holds that draw long enough; if not, it trips. A peak or surge figure with no time on it can't tell you that, which is why this table ranks by watts a station was rated or seen to hold.

Only DJI states a duration. For the original DJI Power 1000, DJI's spec page says the 120 V DYM1000L holds 2,600 W for 30 seconds and the 230 V DYM1000H for 60 seconds, measured in DJI's lab at about 25 °C (77 °F) and 50% battery, and that the time varies with battery temperature and charge. Its 4,400 W peak carries no time. The V2 lifts 2,600 W to its continuous rating, per DJI as quoted by The Technology Man; DJI's US spec page for the V2 is offline, so the V2 figures here come from The Technology Man and OutdoorGearLab. EcoFlow (3,600 W), Anker (3,000 W), OUPES (4,500 W) and BLUETTI (3,600 W in its blog) give surge figures with no time.

Named results. The Technology Man ramped a load on the DJI Power 1000 V2 until it beeped at about 2,900 W and cut out just over 3,000 W, and it started his induction-motor bandsaw but not his table saw. The Solar Lab held the EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus at 2,600 W for about a minute, 800 W over its rating, and saw it shut down almost at once above that. The Solar Lab also found the OUPES Mega 1 lowers its voltage during surges rather than going briefly past 2,000 W. CleanTechnica's Paul Fosse saw the BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 shut down under about 2,700 W of kitchen appliances (his estimate) until he switched on Power Lifting.

Boost modes are not surge. BLUETTI's Lifting Power lowers the voltage so a heater or kettle over the rating runs at reduced power; in Fosse's words, it "does not lift power". It does nothing for a motor that needs full voltage to start.

Not recommended

The OUPES Mega 1 bought for its 4,500 W surge. It has the biggest advertised surge per pound (162 W/lb), but OUPES gives that surge no time, and The Solar Lab saw the voltage sag during surges instead. Its 2,000 W rating works out to 72 W/lb, behind the DJI, EcoFlow and Anker. The BLUETTI Elite 30 V2 for motors: its 1,500 W is Lifting Power, not surge, and its rating is 600 W.
